title: Global Liquidity Peaks: The More Aggressively You Spent on AI in H1, the Sooner You Get Discounted
dek: A stock market rally needs new money to keep buying. Global liquidity is already showing signs of peaking, and the companies that most aggressively invested in AI in the first half are now being discounted rather than rewarded.
why: This episode puts US AI capex, Hong Kong IPO activity, and household balance sheets on the same funding chain, offering a macro framework that does not treat AI as a cure-all.
who: For investors tracking both US AI and China/Hong Kong asset allocation, and for primary market practitioners judging the source and pace of hot money in 2025.
skip: The discussion of specific Hong Kong IPO cases can be skipped; the main thread resumes at 8:11 with the Nvidia liquidity experiment.

points.h: Low IPO break rate is not a good sign
points.body: Do not take the low break rate of Hong Kong IPOs as a sign of market strength. In the first half of this year, the break rate was only around 10-20%, far below the normal level of roughly half-and-half under a market-driven mechanism, meaning the participants were mainly short-term speculative arbitrage funds, not long-term investors. Recently, the supply of new listings has decreased, and some IPO-related funds have had problems, but the two newly listed companies still broke their issue price, showing that temporary supply-side controls have not solved the fundamental problem: Hong Kong also faces peaking liquidity.

points.h: The more aggressive the AI spending, the sooner the punishment
points.body: Market sentiment reversed within a quarter. Before Q1, the capital market rewarded aggression: the louder the AI capex talk, the higher the valuation. By the end of July, when half-year reports were released, any major internet company that had made aggressive capital expenditures in H1—especially those that had burned through free cash flow—was discounted, and even Google was not exempt. Q2 was the quarter of maximum FOMO across the supply chain; everyone rushed to spend before prices rose, and inventory still supported gross margins. By Q3, inventory is depleted and the impact of price increases returns, so the negative factors will appear together.

points.h: Nvidia is closer to Cisco in 2000
points.body: Nvidia's earnings look good, but its cash flow is changing. Before the dot-com bubble burst in 2000, Cisco launched a 'lease-to-own' program to help customers finance purchases, recognizing future revenue as sales upfront. Nvidia is now also pushing lease-to-own. In its earnings report, free cash flow fell by half quarter-over-quarter, and accounts receivable are far above historical levels—which is speculated to be partly related to the credit enhancement and payment structure from lease-to-own. So Nvidia may have reached a point where it needs more aggressive financial measures to maintain capital market expectations, similar to Cisco's situation back then.

points.h: Primary market money comes from bullets three years ago
points.body: The answer lies in the timing of fund raises. The money that will be deployed aggressively in AI and robotics from H2 2025 to H1 2026 mainly comes from funds raised at the market peak in 2020-2022. From 2023 to 2025, they barely invested, until they saw state capital placing bets during a period when no one dared to invest and making the most money—the stories of ChangXin and ChangCun, two large language models, and two major chip companies stimulated market-based funds. The mentality is: copy the homework of state capital. So this is not a rational long-term increment, but more like a delayed emotional release.

points.h: New property policy removes households from the financing chain
points.body: The key of recent property policy is not to rescue developers, but to detach households from the old financing cycle. In the past, buying off-plan housing meant households played the role of financing counterparties in the investment-driven chain: paying first, receiving the property later. The policy pushes the chain toward marketization, so buyers purchase completed homes and only assume the consumer role, with risk reset to developers and financing institutions. The policy was introduced when house prices were near the bottom, to first stabilize the denominator on the asset side and avoid panic from breaking the chain during a decline. Japan after the 1990s and the consolidation of China's coal and mining industries followed similar paths.

points.h: Slow bull is not a slogan but a chip structure
points.body: A slow bull is not achieved by shouting but by layering market chips by duration: at the bottom are low-valuation, high-dividend blue chips held by insurers as long-term money that rarely trades; above that are public funds and index funds, functioning close to a price stabilization role; China Securities Finance and Central Huijin adjust the index at a higher level; and at the top are retail investors, private funds, and active management money. New insurance regulations require liabilities and assets to match in duration, yield, and liquidity, effectively ensuring that long money invests long, medium money invests medium, and short money invests short—not allowing short-term household money to be invested in ten-year illiquid assets.

points.h: Crises grow with each bailout; at least one and a half bubbles
points.body: Since the dollar left gold in 1971, global central banks have become increasingly accustomed to directly intervening in crises by printing money, with each action faster than the last. The quantitative easing after 2008 was supposed to be cleared during the rate hike cycle, but it was interrupted by political intervention, and then COVID hit in 2020, so an even larger wave of money printing was layered on before the previous bubble had dissipated—today we have accumulated at least one and a half bubbles. Central bank governors have learned to print even more money immediately when a crisis emerges, and the endogenous result is that inflation, financial asset appreciation, and wealth inequality all intensify simultaneously. As long as the bubble is not allowed to clear, the world may experience some form of prolonged stagflation.

Fear of missing out: the fear of missing profits others are making, prompting the entire supply chain to spend before prices rise.

The capital market still thinks whoever spends aggressively is great, but when half-year reports come out, it becomes: whoever is aggressive gets punished.
Perhaps Nvidia has also reached a point where, in some sense, it needs to use lease-to-own to drive revenue growth and meet capital market expectations.
Everyone sees that you can pull off this story, so they think, 'I can definitely pull off this story too'—that's roughly the psychology.
